note: Provisional: the owner's disposition outranks the judge's.

verdicts.reason: reset_password.html:7 uses `url_for(..., _external=True)`. `config.py:10` makes SERVER_NAME optional, and nginx uses `server_name _` with `proxy_set_header Host $host` (nginx:4,13,27) and sends no X-Forwarded-Proto, with no ProxyFix, so Host poisoning and http links are possible when SERVER_NAME is unset. It needs an attacker-crafted request and a victim who clicks, so P2 fits better.

routes.py:219-227 is a GET route that calls `launch_task` and commits, so a cross-site GET can enqueue an export. The impact is small (an export of the victim's own posts, with one task at a time), so P3 fits better.
messages.html:11 and 16 both use `href="#"`, so the `prev_url` and `next_url` passed by routes.py:215-216 are never used. Users cannot page through messages.
`requests.post` at translate.py:14-18 has no `timeout`, so a stalled upstream can block a worker. The route is login-protected and has no rate limit, but the practical risk is modest.

auth/routes.py:76-82 sets the password without invalidating anything. `verify_reset_password_token` (models.py:187-193) only checks the signature and expiry (`exp` set at models.py:183), so the token can be reused within 10 minutes.
config.py:9 falls back to the hard-coded 'you-will-never-guess', which signs both Flask sessions and the reset JWTs (models.py:184). A deployment that omits SECRET_KEY can have both forged.
The Dockerfile has no `USER` instruction before `ENTRYPOINT ["./boot.sh"]` (line 16), so the container runs as root. This is a hardening gap rather than an exploitable flaw, so P3 fits better.
